plain_english:
We'll be happy with whatever wealth we have if we've learned to enjoy living simply. Without this skill, no amount of money is enough. With it, any amount is plenty. The best part is that the solution is always within reach. Even poverty can become wealth if you add some thrift to it.

Let's get used to ignoring flashy displays. Judge things by how useful they are, not by how fancy they look. Use food to satisfy hunger, drink to quench thirst, and keep your desires within reasonable limits. Learn to use your body properly. Dress and live the way our ancestors did — the way that actually worked — instead of chasing every new trend.

Learn to be more self-controlled. Push back against luxury. Put limits on your pride. Cool down your anger. Look at poverty without bias. Practice thrift, even though many people are embarrassed to do it. Use simple, cheap solutions for what your body actually needs. Lock up those wild hopes and dreams that have no discipline behind them. Make it your job to get your riches from yourself, not from luck.
original_excerpt: We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid of thrift can convert itself into riches. Let us accustom ourselves to set aside mere outward show, and to measure things by their uses, not by their ornamental trappings: let our hunger be tamed by food, our thirst quenched by drinking, our lust confined within needful bounds; let us learn to use our limbs, and to arrange our dress and way of life according to what was approved of by our ancestors, not in imitation of new-fangled models: let us learn to increase our continence, to repress luxury, to set bounds to our pride, to assuage our anger, to look upon poverty without prejudice, to practise thrift, albeit many are ashamed to do so, to apply cheap remedies to the wants of nature, to keep all undisciplined hopes and aspirations as it were under lock and key, and to make it our business to get our riches from ourselves and not from Fortune.

plain_english: We can never fully protect ourselves from all the bad luck that threatens us. If we spread ourselves too thin, we'll feel the impact of every storm. We need to keep our lives simple and focused, so Fortune's arrows can't find their mark. Sometimes small setbacks actually help us. And serious problems are often cured by lighter ones. When your mind won't listen to good advice and gentler methods don't work, why not consider that poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin might actually be serving your best interests? Sometimes one trouble cancels out another.
original_excerpt: We never can so thoroughly defeat the vast diversity and malignity of misfortune with which we are threatened as not to feel the weight of many gusts if we offer a large spread of canvas to the wind: we must draw our affairs into a small compass, to make the darts of Fortune of no avail. For this reason, sometimes slight mishaps have turned into remedies, and more serious disorders have been healed by slighter ones. When the mind pays no attention to good advice, and cannot be brought to its senses by milder measures, why should we not think that its interests are being served by poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin being applied to it? one evil is balanced by another.

plain_english: Let's learn to eat dinner without needing all of Rome to watch us. Let's have fewer servants bossing us around. Let's buy clothes that actually serve their purpose. Let's live in smaller houses. In chariot races, the smart driver takes the inside track. The same goes for life itself. Even books and learning — the most respectable way for a gentleman to spend money — only make sense if you don't go overboard.
original_excerpt: Let us then teach ourselves to be able to dine without all Rome to look on, to be the slaves of fewer slaves, to get clothes which fulfil their original purpose, and to live in a smaller house. The inner curve is the one to take, not only in running races and in the contests of the circus, but also in the race of life; even literary pursuits, the most becoming thing for a gentleman to spend money upon, are only justifiable as long as they are kept within bounds.

plain_english: What's the point of owning countless books and libraries when you can barely read through all the titles in a lifetime? A student gets overwhelmed by such a huge collection instead of learning from it. It's much better to focus on a few good writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books burned at Alexandria. Some people praised this library as a wonderful monument to royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who called it "a splendid result of the kings' taste and careful attention." But it had nothing to do with taste or care. It was just scholarly showing off — not even scholarly, really, since they collected books not to learn but to impress people. Many men know less about literature than we'd expect from a slave, yet they use their books not for study but as dining room decorations.
original_excerpt: What is the use of possessing numberless books and libraries, whose titles their owner can hardly read through in a lifetime? A student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books were burned at Alexandria: some would have praised this library as a most noble memorial of royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who says that it was "a splendid result of the taste and attentive care of the kings." It had nothing to do with taste or care, but was a piece of learned luxury, nay, not even learned, since they amassed it, not for the sake of learning, but to make a show, like many men who know less about letters than a slave is expected to know, and who uses his books not to help him in his studies but to ornament his dining-room.

plain_english: Get as many books as you want, but don't buy them just to show off. "It's better," you say, "to spend money on books than on fancy bronze vases and paintings." Not really. Anything taken to excess is wrong. What's your excuse for someone who buys ivory and exotic wood bookcases, collects works by unknown or terrible authors, and sits yawning among thousands of books? He likes their spines and titles more than what's actually inside them. You'll find this in the homes of the laziest people — shelves packed floor to ceiling with works by every famous speaker and historian. These days a library has become as essential to a house as hot and cold running water. I'd forgive them if they were really obsessed with reading. But they're not. These expensive works of brilliant minds, with all their beautiful illustrations, are just bought for show — fancy wall decorations.
original_excerpt: Let a man, then, obtain as many books as he wants, but none for show. "It is more respectable," say you, "to spend one's money on such books than on vases of Corinthian brass and paintings." Not so: everything that is carried to excess is wrong. What excuses can you find for a man who is eager to buy bookcases of ivory and citrus wood, to collect the works of unknown or discredited authors, and who sits yawning amid so many thousands of books, whose backs and titles please him more than any other part of them? Thus in the houses of the laziest of men you will see the works of all the orators and historians stacked upon book-shelves reaching right up to the ceiling. At the present day a library has become as necessary an appendage to a house as a hot and cold bath. I would excuse them straightway if they really were carried away by an excessive zeal for literature; but as it is, these costly works of sacred genius, with all the illustrations that adorn them, are merely bought for display and to serve as wall-furniture.
